opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a pretty big shift for me. I come from a theoretical computer science background, so for a long time I thought of competition math and olympiad programming as a kind of gold standard for careful, creative reasoning. These are problems where you can't just pattern-match; you have to explore, make mistakes, backtrack, and eventually find an idea that actually works. When models started performing at that level at IOI and IMO, my first reaction was a mix of excitement and a little disbelief.

What it changed for me was the sense of what's *tractable*. Before, I thought deep reasoning might require some fundamentally new architecture or some clever symbolic machinery bolted on. Seeing these results made me take much more seriously the idea that general methods, scaling reinforcement learning on reasoning, letting the model think longer and verify its own work, can get surprisingly far. It reframed the question from "can models reason?" to "how far does this go, and where does it break?"

It also made me want to work on it more directly. Competitions are a wonderful benchmark, but they're still a contained world: the problems are well-posed, there's a known answer, and the time horizon is a few hours. Real research is messier. You don't know whether the problem is even solvable, the right formulation is half the work, and progress can take months. So for me the natural next step is pushing reasoning toward that regime, helping models make genuine contributions to open problems in math and theoretical CS, and getting better at checking their own claims so we can actually trust the results.

So I'd say it moved me from being an interested observer to thinking this is one of the most exciting places to be. If models can already do olympiad-level reasoning, the question of whether they can become real research collaborators feels very concrete now, not science fiction.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the breakthroughs made him want to work on reasoning more directly, but it does not state that making models smarter could have greater impact than continuing his academic career.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, those results shifted something pretty fundamental for me, and I'll try to explain why.

I came up through theoretical computer science, complexity theory specifically. In that world, you spend your life thinking about what computation can and can't do, and you develop a certain skepticism. You see a lot of claims, and most of them don't hold up under pressure. So for a long time, when people said models were "reasoning," my instinct was to say, well, show me something I can't explain away as pattern matching on the training distribution.

The IMO and IOI results were hard to explain away. These are problems designed by people whose entire job is to construct things that haven't been seen before. Olympiad problems are adversarial by construction. And the model wasn't retrieving solutions, it was producing multi-step arguments that held together, with the kind of case analysis and backtracking that you see in a strong human competitor. I was a competitive programmer myself, so I know what those problems feel like from the inside, and I know how much they resist shortcuts.

What changed in my thinking was less "the model is smart now" and more that I stopped treating reasoning as a far-off target and started treating it as a thing we can actually study and improve, systematically, today. That's a big shift. In theory, you often work on questions where the honest answer is "we may never know." Here, there's a feedback loop. You have a hypothesis about what the model is missing, you can test it, and you find out in weeks instead of decades.

The other thing it did was make me take the open questions more seriously, not less. If the model can do olympiad math, then the gap between that and doing research mathematics, or finding a new algorithm, is a real scientific question. What's the nature of that gap? Is it search depth, is it the ability to build and maintain abstractions over a long horizon, is it something about knowing which problems are worth working on? Those feel like questions a theorist can actually contribute to, and that's what pulled me in. I didn't want to watch from the outside anymore.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the results drew him into studying and improving reasoning models, but does not state that making models smarter might have greater impact on the world than continuing his academic career.

astra-6.text:
It made me more optimistic about what reasoning models can do, but it also sharpened the question of what comes next. These competitions are very demanding, yet they give you a clearly stated problem with a solution you know exists. In research, you often don’t have either of those things. You have to decide what question to ask, which direction is promising, and when to abandon an approach.

So I see those results as a strong motivation to pursue reasoning research. Can we move from solving a difficult problem that someone has prepared to exploring a question where nobody knows the answer? That’s the transition I find especially exciting.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the competition results motivated reasoning research and highlights moving toward open-ended research questions. It does not say that making models smarter could have greater impact than continuing an academic career.

sol-6.1.text:
It made me update on how far these models can go with reasoning. Problems at the level of the IMO or IOI require more than knowing a lot of facts—you have to find an approach, work through it, and sometimes realize that it’s wrong and start again. Seeing models succeed there made the progress feel much more concrete.

But I wouldn’t take that as a reason to stop pursuing reasoning research. For me, it makes the questions more interesting: What is driving that progress? Where does it generalize, and where does it break? And can we turn the ability to solve a well-defined competition problem into the ability to make progress on an open-ended research question? That’s a much bigger challenge.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses how model successes shaped his interest in reasoning research, but does not say that making models smarter could have greater impact than continuing his academic career.
